problem: Existing embodied-AI simulators (Habitat, AI2-THOR, Matterport3D, iGibson) focus on household settings and lack retail-specific environments with diverse, readable products, checkout interaction, and human baselines for shopping tasks.
motivation: Retail is a large real-world application area (stocking, product comparison, checkout) where agents need fine-grained perception (reading labels, expiry dates, barcodes), navigation and manipulation. A photorealistic retail sandbox with VR human demonstrations allows controlled benchmarking of embodied agents against humans.
key_idea: Build a Unity-based photorealistic convenience-store simulator (250 scanned grocery products, 3 layouts, self-checkout, VR + Python WebSocket API) together with SariBench, human VR demonstrations over easy/average/difficult shopping tasks, plus a baseline VLM agent.
insight: Human vs. agent comparison shows a large gap even on easy tasks: the Gemini 2.5 Pro ReAct-style agent takes up to ~16x longer and succeeds 33-69% vs. humans 89-100%. This shows the sandbox is solvable but hard, and that VLM latency, reasoning and decision-making are bottlenecks. The OCR analysis (P 0.986, R 0.943, CER 0.014) shows textures are readable, but rotated or stylized text degrades OCR, so agents need active viewpoint control.
method: Product assets: 250 real-packaged grocery items in 11 categories, scanned labels modeled in Blender; simple/complex/deformable meshes; JPG textures, LOD, box colliders; annotated with price, ingredients, nutrition, allergens, origin.

Dynamic elements: barcode planes with ray-cast scanning, expiration dates rendered with URP decals randomly generated per session, price tags updating with randomized, category-grouped product placement.

Environment: three store layouts from surveys of local convenience stores, fridge cabinets with hinged/sliding doors, self-checkout with touchscreen and barcode scanner; frustum and occlusion culling.
Avatar & VR: camera + two hands in a character controller; VR hand interaction, haptics, tunneling vignette, teleportation; camera at 1.6 m when no headset.
Python API: JSON commands over WebSocket to a C# Unity server (TransformAgent, TransformHands, grips, pokes, RequestScreenshot, Reset).
SariBench: easy/average/difficult tasks; 100 VR demonstration videos from 20 participants with head/hand pose, grip state, held item at 10 fps and think-aloud transcripts.

Baseline agent: Gemini 2.5 Pro with associative-learning step (mode/context cues from semantic and episodic memory), planning step emitting action sequences, execution parser; tools loc_object (VLM bbox), PaddleOCR, Depth-Anything-V2-Small.

setting.backbone: Gemini 2.5 Pro (gemini-2.5-pro-preview-05-06, frozen, 2048 reasoning token budget) + PaddleOCR + Depth-Anything-V2 Small
setting.observation: first-person monocular RGB screenshots plus avatar coordinates
setting.action_space: low-level API: move_forward 0.1 units, pan ±2.5°, strafe, hand transforms, grip toggle; high-level center_object_on_screen and retrieve_item
setting.privileged: semantic memory text file with store layout, product-to-shelf locations and directions from spawn point

numbers_note: Not a standard navigation benchmark; only easy-task agent results are reported. Human results (HAT/HCR for all 9 difficulty-layout cells) are not agent results. Environment metrics: FPS 26.73/23.23/35.14; OCR precision 0.986, recall 0.943, CER 0.014.
results: Humans complete easy tasks in 47-73 s with 88.88-100% completion, while the Gemini 2.5 Pro agent needs 420-780 s and completes only 33.33-68.63%. Average and difficult tasks were evaluated only with humans (85-158 s, 87.5-100% completion). The environment runs at only 23-35 FPS on a GTX 1080.
limitations: Agent evaluated only on easy tasks; the agent is a simple proof-of-concept with no checkout or multi-item handling and is very slow.
Performance below the 60 FPS target; rigid-body-only products with box colliders, no deformables; only 250 food products and 3 small layouts.
Small human study (20 participants, 100 videos), motion sickness reported; success judged by manual inspection.
